The majority voted to pass the [bill](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5714) in the Senate. Since the bill had already passed in the House of Representatives, it will now become law. In parliamentary jargon, the Members of Parliament (MPs) voted to [read the bill for a third time](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ### What does the bill do? The bill is rather technical. According to the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1617a/17bd023), its purpose is to: * *clarify apportionment arrangements relating to certain petroleum deposits that straddle state and Commonwealth jurisdictions*; and * *ensure the capacity of the [National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Environmental Management Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Offshore_Petroleum_Safety_and_Environmental_Management_Authority) (NOPSEMA) to refund fees paid to it where necessary*.

The bill amends the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Act to allow apportionment agreements for multiple petroleum pools across jurisdictional boundaries, ensuring the validity of agreements such as the Torosa gas field apportionment, and clarifies regulation-making powers for refunding environment plan and safety case levies.

The speaker supported the Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Amendment (Petroleum Pools and Other Measures) Bill 2016, which provides royalty certainty for multiple petroleum pools straddling Commonwealth-state boundaries, particularly for the Browse Basin project. The speaker also criticised Western Australia Nationals leader Brendon Grylls' proposed $5-per-tonne iron ore mining tax, arguing it would destroy jobs, undermine investment certainty, and fail to address state budget issues.

The Offshore Petroleum and Greenhouse Gas Storage Amendment (Petroleum Pools and Other Measures) Bill 2016 was commended, with amendments ensuring the ongoing validity of apportionment agreements under section 54 of the OPGGS Act for areas with multiple petroleum pools, and providing a clear regulation-making power for refunds and remittal of environmental plan levies and safety case levies for the National Offshore Petroleum Safety and Environmental Management Authority. Defence of Western Australian Nationals leader Brendon Grylls was made against disparaging remarks, while Western Australian Labor leader Mark McGowan was criticised for having no vision, plan or policies ahead of the 11 March 2017 state election.
